title: The Search for the Wicked Witch, part 9
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from The Wonderful Wizard of Oz by L. Frank Baum (1900).
body: Dorothy’s life became very sad as she grew to understand that it would be harder than ever to get back to Kansas and Aunt Em again. Sometimes she would cry bitterly for hours, with Toto sitting at her feet and looking into her face, whining dismally to show how sorry he was for his little mistress. Toto did not really care whether he was in Kansas or the Land of Oz so long as Dorothy was with him; but he knew the little girl was unhappy, and that made him unhappy too.

Now the Wicked Witch had a great longing to have for her own the Silver Shoes which the girl always wore. Her bees and her crows and her wolves were lying in heaps and drying up, and she had used up all the power of the Golden Cap; but if she could only get hold of the Silver Shoes, they would give her more power than all the other things she had lost. She watched Dorothy carefully, to see if she ever took off her shoes, thinking she might steal them. But the child was so proud of her pretty shoes that she never took them off except at night and when she took her bath. The Witch was too much afraid of the dark to dare go in Dorothy’s room at night to take the shoes, and her dread of water was greater than her fear of the dark, so she never came near when Dorothy was bathing. Indeed, the old Witch never touched water, nor ever let water touch her in any way.

But the wicked creature was very cunning, and she finally thought of a trick that would give her what she wanted. She placed a bar of iron in the middle of the kitchen floor, and then by her magic arts made the iron invisible to human eyes. So that when Dorothy walked across the floor she stumbled over the bar, not being able to see it, and fell at full length. She was not much hurt, but in her fall one of the Silver Shoes came off; and before she could reach it, the Witch had snatched it away and put it on her own skinny foot.

The wicked woman was greatly pleased with the success of her trick, for as long as she had one of the shoes she owned half the power of their charm, and Dorothy could not use it against her, even had she known how to do so.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Wicked Witch want from Dorothy?
options: The Silver Shoes
The Golden Cap
Toto
The basket of food

questions.prompt: Per the passage, when did Dorothy take off her shoes?
options: Only at night and when she bathed
Only when she slept outdoors
She never took them off at all
Whenever she crossed water

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why didn't the Witch enter Dorothy's room at night to steal the shoes?
options: She was too afraid of the dark
The door was locked
Toto guarded the room
She had no reason to go there

questions.prompt: Per the passage, where did the Witch place the bar of iron?
options: In the middle of the kitchen floor
Just outside Dorothy's bedroom door
Beside the water bucket
Under Dorothy's bed

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how did the Witch make the iron bar dangerous to Dorothy?
options: She made it invisible with magic
She heated it red hot
She balanced it on a shelf above the door
She hid it under a rug

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why did the Witch never come near Dorothy while she was bathing?
options: Her dread of water was greater than her fear of the dark
She was busy tending her bees and wolves
Dorothy always bathed with Toto nearby
She had already given up on the shoes

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why did losing just one Silver Shoe still benefit the Witch?
options: Owning one shoe gave her half the power of their charm
She could sell the shoe for gold
It matched her own missing shoe
It let her fly instead of the other creatures

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why couldn't the Witch's bees, crows, and wolves help her get the shoes?
options: They were lying in heaps and drying up
They had flown away to the Emerald City
Dorothy had already defeated them
They refused to obey her anymore

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the overall point of the passage?
options: The Witch tricked Dorothy with an invisible obstacle and gained power from the shoe she stole
Dorothy escaped the Witch's castle without incident
The Witch lost all her remaining power trying to steal the shoes
Toto distracted the Witch long enough for Dorothy to hide the shoes

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean that the Witch was "cunning"?
options: Clever in a deceitful way
Physically powerful
Honest and straightforward
Easily frightened

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did Toto do to show he was sorry for Dorothy?
options: He whined dismally
He barked at the Witch
He hid under the bed
He ran away to find help

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what had happened to the power of the Golden Cap?
options: The Witch had used up all of it
Dorothy had taken it from her
It had never had any power
It only worked underwater

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what happened to Dorothy when she stumbled over the invisible bar?
options: She fell at full length
She twisted her ankle badly
She dropped her basket of food
She caught herself before falling

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what did the Witch do with the shoe once she snatched it?
options: Put it on her own foot
Locked it in a chest
Threw it into the fire
Buried it in the garden

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why did the Witch watch Dorothy carefully day to day?
options: To see if she ever took off her shoes, so she could steal them
To make sure Dorothy did her chores
To learn how Dorothy had killed her sister
To find out if Toto could talk

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes how the Witch's trick worked?
options: An invisible obstacle made Dorothy trip so a shoe would come off
The Witch simply asked Dorothy to hand over a shoe
The Witch waited until Dorothy fell asleep to take the shoe
The Witch traded the Golden Cap for one of the shoes

questions.prompt: As used in the passage, what does it mean that Dorothy was "proud" of her pretty shoes?
options: She took great satisfaction and delight in them
She was embarrassed to wear them
She wanted to trade them away
She had forgotten she owned them
